items.abstract: Building on recent research from the eastern Mediterranean hinterlands in the scope of the Middle Pleistocene, it is now possible to ascertain different scenarios of hominin population dynamics, as well as the spread of innovations in human subsistence strategies along with lithic technology. Based on fossil evidence, Neanderthals likely originated in western Europe. By contrast, non-Levallois Quina-type lithic assemblages appear to have first originated in the Levant within the Yabrudian technological complex. The earliest confirmed Neanderthal remains in the eastern Mediterranean, associated with the early appearance of Quina-type artifacts in Europe, were found in the Central Balkans, at the site of Velika Balanica. Here, we present a comparison of cervid processing at Velika Balanica as a reference point, and compare it with Levantine and some northern Mediterranean sites of similar age with Quina elements in the lithic industry, as various cervids were a common main subsistence resource linking these sites. Cervid carcass processing at all these sites appears to have been complete, not as a response to population pressure or starvation, but rather because cervid marrow offers a distinct nutrient profile compared to other available large mammals. This marrow alone provides a combination of essential nutrients that would otherwise require exploiting multiple species, thereby reducing the energetic costs associated with search, hunting, and processing.

items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    The postglacial evolution of High Arctic coastal environments is recorded in the rich fossiliferous archives of raised marine terraces. This study employs a multi‐proxy approach combining molluscan community analysis, taphonomy and sedimentology to reconstruct the Early to Mid‐Holocene environmental dynamics of the Mimerdalen embayment in the Billefjorden area of central Svalbard. Our results indicate that local benthic succession was driven by a complex interplay of glacio‐isostatic rebound and fluctuating sediment supply rather than simple climatic warming. We identify a four‐stage evolutionary trajectory: (1) an initial glaciomarine, brackish‐water phase dominated by the pioneer taxa
                    <jats:italic>Mya truncata</jats:italic>
                    and
                    <jats:italic>Hiatella arctica</jats:italic>
                    ; (2) a transition to fully marine conditions that facilitated the expansion of thermophilous species (
                    <jats:italic>Mytilus edulis</jats:italic>
                    and
                    <jats:italic>Arctica islandica</jats:italic>
                    ); (3) a return to restricted brackish conditions due to forced regression and basin shallowing; and (4) a transition towards modern open‐fjord equilibrium, as slower glacio‐isostatic uplift and Mid‐Holocene Neoglacial cooling led to the disappearance of the thermally demanding taxa. Although not directly radiocarbon dated, valves of
                    <jats:italic>Arctica islandica</jats:italic>
                    and
                    <jats:italic>Zirfaea crispata</jats:italic>
                    are stratigraphically associated with dated
                    <jats:italic>M. truncata</jats:italic>
                    , suggesting their presence as early as ~10.4 cal. ka BP. This potentially advances their known regional arrival by up to 600 and 300 years, respectively, with
                    <jats:italic>A. islandica</jats:italic>
                    persisting until ~7.7 cal. ka BP. Comparisons with the Kapp Ekholm reference section demonstrate that local geomorphological stability and ephemeral disturbances, such as hyperpycnal deltaic input, were critical drivers of biodiversity, enabling the establishment of thermally demanding species. Ultimately, our findings confirm that Early Holocene sea temperatures significantly exceeded modern values, while emphasizing the overwhelming importance of salinity and seabed stability in shaping molluscan ecological structure. This study underscores the crucial role of local environmental heterogeneity in modulating the biological response to regional Holocene climate forcing in the High Arctic.
                  </jats:p>
authors: Martin Lulák, Martin Hanáček, Slavomír Nehyba, Tomáš Weiner, Daniel Nývlt

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Glacial/interglacial climate cycles since marine isotope stage (MIS) 12 influenced the discontinuous and 73 m‐long sediment record from the volcanic crater of Rodderberg in the East Eifel Volcanic Field, Germany. High‐resolution grain size and geochemical data have been valued by numerical dating techniques (radiocarbon and luminescence dating, tephrochronology), providing an environmental reconstruction since the Middle Pleistocene (439 ka). The observed hydroclimatic variability, along with silting‐up of the crater basin, significantly influenced depositional processes. This results in the formation of laminated, sand‐rich, and organic‐rich sediments during interglacial periods, as well as layered, silt‐rich minerogenic loess derivatives during glacial periods. According to chronology, the crater basin desiccated during MIS 8 and MIS 5, causing erosion of the interglacials related to MIS 9 and MIS 5e. The combined evidence over five glacial/interglacial cycles suggests a depositional evolution from a deep crater lake during MIS 12–10, desiccation during MIS 8 with erosion of MIS 9, a shallow lake for MIS 7, and a desiccating wetland during MIS 6, followed by deposition of loess (MIS 6‐2) and a Holocene soil (MIS 1).</jats:p>

items.abstract: The Silurian Ockerkalk of Sardinia (Italy): Stratigraphy, palaeontology, mineralogy and geological significance Ferretti, Annalisa; Malferrari, Daniele; Corriga, Maria Giovanna; Corradini, Carlo Newsletters on Stratigraphy, (2026), p. - Abstract The Ockerkalk is an informal ochre-coloured calcareous unit widely distributed across Europe and represents a key upper Silurian (Ludlow–Přídolí) stratigraphical interval, occurring in Thuringia (Germany), Sardinia (Italy), the Pyrenees (Spain), and the Czech Republic. Among these regions, the Silius–Gerrei area of southeastern Sardinia preserves one of the most complete and continuous Ockerkalk successions, where exceptionally well-exposed stratigraphical sections provide a unique record of late Silurian marine environments. The abundance of conodont faunas, together with the excellent preservation of sedimentary structures, makes this area particularly valuable for reconstructing late Silurian palaeoenvironmental conditions within a high-resolution biostratigraphical framework. Despite its wide geographical distribution, the overall stratigraphical significance and broader geological importance of the Ockerkalk have never been comprehensively evaluated. This study addresses this gap by integrating current knowledge of the unit’s lithostratigraphy, palaeontological content, and depositional architecture within a broader geological framework. A detailed mineralogical investigation is also carried out to identify the compositional and diagenetic factors responsible for the distinctive ochre coloration of the Ockerkalk and to assess their variation throughout the succession. By integrating lithostratigraphical observations, biostratigraphical constraints, and mineralogical and geochemical analyses, this study refines the stratigraphical framework of the Ockerkalk in Sardinia and clarifies its relationships with coeval peri-Gondwanan carbonate facies. The Ockerkalk records low-energy carbonate deposition in a moderately deep pelagic to hemipelagic setting with intermittent siliciclastic input, while its conodont biozones provide a robust high-resolution chronostratigraphical framework from the upper Gorstian to the upper Přídolí, demonstrating that the unit does not extend to the Silurian–Devonian boundary. Mineralogical and geochemical data show that the unit is strongly calcite-dominated (83.5–95.5 wt%), with subordinate illite and quartz and minor Fe-rich amorphous material concentrated in coatings and veins, indicating a significant post-depositional overprint related to thermal alteration and structurally controlled fluid circulation.

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    The Mesoamerican Preclassic period offers a laboratory for understanding how interactions between climate and early human occupation have shaped tropical ecosystems. Although the environmental history of the Maya lowlands during this period is relatively well known, mid‐elevation regions remain poorly understood. Here, we present a multiproxy sedimentary analysis from Lake Nahá, tropical mountains of southeastern Mexico, to elucidate climate–human interactions. Our results reveal three environmental stages that broadly align with the cultural–historical phases of the period. The first stage (~3200–2680 cal a BP) features low lake levels, high aquatic productivity, a progressively drier climate, and sparse human occupation. The second stage (~2680–2170 cal a BP) shows rising lake levels that expanded aquatic habitats, coinciding with a pause in the drying trend and greater anthropogenic impact. The third stage (~2170–1600 cal a BP) records renewed drying, lower lake levels, and moderate primary productivity, alongside a decline in fire activity and a shift toward more negative δ
                    <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                    C, coincident with the large‐scale Preclassic abandonment. These results demonstrate that Preclassic environmental trajectories in the tropical mountains were shaped by the combined influence of hydroclimate variability, coherent with that reported for the Maya lowlands, and spatially heterogeneous human occupation.
                  </jats:p>
